title: How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualised
text:
On 28 February 2026, the US and Israel began large-scale strikes on Iran. Tehran responded by attacking Israeli and US allies across the Gulf.
Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, was killed on the first day of strikes, and the strait of Hormuz – a crucial waterway for transporting oil – was effectively closed soon after. The conflict quickly became a regional war with global economic consequences.
Since then, bursts of fighting have repeatedly given way to ceasefires and negotiations. Each diplomatic opening has been followed by fresh threats, disputed agreements and renewed attacks.
The strait of Hormuz remains at the centre of the conflict. In normal times, more than 100 vessels passed through the narrow waterway each day, carrying about a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade. Any closure or attack on shipping can disrupt global supplies and send prices higher.
This timeline traces six months of strikes, public threats and failed diplomacy - and shows how the war has disrupted shipping and driven swings in the oil price.
Early morning on 28 February, the US and Israel launch a joint campaign of large-scale strikes across Iran. Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei is killed in these opening strikes. Oil was trading below $70 a barrel, but began to climb as the scale of the attack became clear.
February daily average: 110
The charts track oil prices and reported US and Israeli and Iranian drone, missile and artillery attacks. Social posts come from the US president, Donald Trump, US Central Command (CENTCOM) — which oversees US military operations across much of the Middle East — and Iranian officials and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), an elite force that answers to the supreme leader. Israeli actions appear in the narrative and strike data, but Israeli government posts are not reproduced.
Iran responds to the opening bombardment with missile and drone strikes against Israel, the UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. Striking several neighbouring states directly is seen as a major escalation, turning the conflict into a regional war.
Spokesperson for the General Staff of the Armed Forces: We will teach Israel and America a lesson they have never experienced in their history.
A missile strikes the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in Minab, beside an IRGC naval complex. Amnesty International says 156 people were killed, including 120 children, and that its evidence indicated the US was responsible. The US still has not published a final account. The bombing became the opening phase's deadliest civilian incident and central to Iran's narrative of American aggression.
Iran restricts commercial passage through the strait of Hormuz. In normal times, more than 100 vessels transit the waterway each day, carrying about a quarter of the world's seaborne oil trade. Traffic falls by 80% and oil prices climb sharply, turning control of the strait into one of Iran's main sources of global economic leverage.
February daily average: 110
Mojtaba Khamenei is chosen as Iran's new supreme leader after the killing of his father, Ali Khamenei. The rapid succession suggests continuity rather than a political reset: Tehran's leadership changes, but its public commitment to retaliation does not. Strikes continued.
With traffic still depressed, Iran asserts the right to approve vessels using Hormuz and Trump threatens Iran's power plants unless passage is resumed. Tehran blames the disruption on US attacks and insurers; Washington blames deliberate Iranian obstruction. Both invoke freedom and security while using the strait as leverage. Trump's warning that a "whole civilization" could die departs sharply from customary diplomatic rhetoric and draws criticism even from Maga-aligned figures.
February daily average: 110
If Iran doesn't FULLY OPEN, WITHOUT THREAT, the Strait of Hormuz, within 48 HOURS from this exact point in time, the United States of America will hit and obliterate their various POWER PLANTS, STARTING WITH THE BIGGEST ONE FIRST!
- Strait of Hormuz is not closed. Ships hesitate because insurers fear the war of choice you initiated—not Iran - No insurer—and no Iranian—will be swayed by more threats. Try respect - Freedom of Navigation cannot exist without Freedom of Trade. Respect both—or expect neither
The United States of America is in serious discussions with A NEW, AND MORE REASONABLE, REGIME to end our Military Operations in Iran. Great progress has been made but, if for any reason a deal is not shortly reached, which it probably will be, and if the Hormuz Strait is not immediately "Open for Business," we will conclude our lovely "stay" in Iran by blowing up and completely obliterating all of their Electric Generating Plants, Oil Wells and Kharg Island (and possibly all desalinization plants!), which we have purposefully not yet "touched." ...
Our operations are aimed at enemy aggressors who have no respect for Arabs or Iranians, nor can provide any security. Just look at what we did to their aerial command.
A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don't want that to happen, but it probably will ...
The US and Iran agree to a two-week conditional ceasefire, including a temporary reopening of the strait of Hormuz, after a last-minute diplomatic intervention led by Pakistan. Oil prices drop.
Ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz must coordinate with the IRGC Navy and use designated alternative routes to ensure maritime safety and avoid the risk of striking anti-ship mines
The diplomatic opening does not produce a settlement. After a 21-hour first day of talks, the US vice-president, JD Vance, says his team is leaving Pakistan without a deal, despite the highest-level direct engagement between Washington and Tehran in decades. The ceasefire reduces attacks, but shipping through Hormuz remains constrained.
February daily average: 110
Iran says Hormuz cannot remain open while the US blockade continued; Trump says the waterway is fully open while confirming the blockade remained. The posts use the same certainty to describe opposite realities. The ceasefire has reduced attacks, but it has not produced a collective understanding.
THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ IS COMPLETELY OPEN AND READY FOR BUSINESS AND FULL PASSAGE, BUT THE NAVAL BLOCKADE WILL REMAIN IN FULL FORCE AND EFFECT AS IT PERTAINS TO IRAN, ONLY ...
Trump extends the ceasefire indefinitely but kept the US naval blockade of Iran in place. Attacks slow and oil prices ease, yet the central dispute is untouched. Washington frames the blockade as enforcing free navigation, while Tehran said there cannot be free passage while Iran itself is blockaded.
I just cancelled the trip of my representatives going to Islamabad, Pakistan, to meet with the Iranians ...
With direct talks stalled, Iran sends a 14-point proposal for ending the war to Pakistani mediators. Trump says he would review it, keeping diplomacy alive even as the two sides remain divided over the blockade, sanctions and the future of the strait of Hormuz.
February daily average: 110
CENTCOM announces a naval mission to escort merchant ships through Hormuz, framing it as the restoration of free navigation. Iran calls the deployment a ceasefire violation and attacks US destroyers after alleging that an Iranian tanker had been struck. Both cast their actions as defensive and the other side as the original aggressor.
Pressure from Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE helps avert another planned US attack. Trump then claims an agreement was largely negotiated; Iran says positions have moved closer but there was no deal. Once again, de-escalation comes through regional mediation and temporary restraint rather than a signed settlement.
Esmaeil Baqaei, Foreign spokesperson: Iran and the US have moved closer on some issues but have not reached an agreement [...] Iran’s immediate priority is ending the war on all fronts, including Lebanon [...] with nuclear negotiations potentially addressed at a later stage [...] The Strait of Hormuz is not a matter for the US and should be dealt with by Iran and other countries bordering the strait.
(...) An Agreement has been largely negotiated, subject to finalization between the United States of America, the Islamic Republic of Iran, and the various other Countries (...) Separately, I had a call with Prime Minister Bibi Netanyahu, of Israel, which, likewise, went very well. Final aspects and details of the Deal are currently being discussed, and will be announced shortly. In addition to many other elements of the Agreement, the Strait of Hormuz will be opened.
As Iranian negotiators travel to Qatar, the US strikes missile launch sites and boats in southern Iran. CENTCOM insists the action did not end the ceasefire. Iran appears to attack a US airbase in Kuwait the next day. The label ‘ceasefire’ now appears to describe only limits on escalation rather than an absence of fighting.
Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi: Communications with the US are continuing, but there has been no tangible progress in negotiations [...] Iran will only return to negotiations if its rights are secured, the war in Lebanon ends and regional tensions are brought to an end.
Iran fires missiles at Israel after Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon; Israel responds, and US forces shoot down Iranian drones near Hormuz. Trump says both sides want peace, while Iran describes diplomacy and military pressure as complementary tools. The language sounds more conciliatory, but the renewed fighting again puts commercial passage through the waterway at risk.
February daily average: 110
Both sides, Israel and Iran, are looking to do an immediate CEASEFIRE! Final negotiations on "Peace" are proceeding, subject to ignorance or stupidity getting in its way. The Blockade will remain in place, and in full force and effect, until a "Final Deal" is reached. Things should move quickly.
Diplomacy and military action must work alongside each other [...] relying on either alone is not enough to defend Iran’s interests [...] Iran can use the threat of military action to advance negotiations and, when necessary, use military force to strengthen its negotiating position [...] We fight when it is time to fight and negotiate when it is time to negotiate.
Iran downs a US Apache helicopter patrolling over the strait of Hormuz. Two days of strikes follow, reversing the brief lull and showing how quickly an incident could overwhelm the diplomatic track.
The United States will be hitting Iran (Whose Navy, Air Force, Radar, Anti Aircraft, and all other forms of Defense, together with most of its offensive capability, are GONE!), VERY HARD TONIGHT.
Based on the fact that discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran have been brought to the highest level of Iranian leadership and approved, I have, as President of the United States of America, cancelled the scheduled strikes and bombings against Iran this evening.
A memorandum establishes 60 days of technical talks and the US removed its blockade. Trump calls the deal complete, but Iran describes a temporary framework that left inspections, sanctions and shipping charges unresolved. Both claim a diplomatic success while presenting incompatible agreements. Meanwhile, oil prices fall.
The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete. Congratulations to all! I hereby fully authorize the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz, and, simultaneously herewith, authorize the immediate removal of the United States Naval blockade. Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!
The Strait of Hormuz will never return to its pre-war conditions [...] Iran has sovereign rights in the strait and will charge for services related to passage [...] with the payment mechanism formalised in an agreement Iran would continue to operate in the strait in accordance with international law and maritime regulations.
Optimism over the memorandum lasts less than two weeks. After attacks in Lebanon, Iran strikes a commercial cargo vessel near Oman and retaliatory attacks follow. Oil prices rebound as the risk to shipping through the strait of Hormuz returns.
February daily average: 110
Mohammad Bagher-Ghalibaf, head of negotiations: Iran will not back down over the Strait of Hormuz [...] Vessels will be allowed to use the strait without paying service fees for 60 days, while Iran has committed to addressing safety issues, including mines, within 30 days [...] Iran and Oman will determine future arrangements for managing the strait and providing maritime services, in line with international law and the sovereign rights of the coastal states.
The US and Iran conduct their largest exchange of fire since the interim deal. The US launches a new wave of strikes, and Iran says it will no longer distinguish between the US and its Gulf allies. Both present escalation as a defensive response to the other's breach, and oil prices rise sharply.
Six days after the ceasefire collapsed, the US reinstates its naval blockade of Iran. Trump calls the US the "guardian" of Hormuz and proposes a 20% cargo charge; Iran adopts the same language to assert its own right to levy fees.
February daily average: 110
The Hormuz Strait is OPEN, and will remain OPEN, with or without Iran. We are reinstating the THE IRANIAN BLOCKADE, so named because it is only stopping Iran's ships or customers from entering or leaving. All other countries will have fair and open use of the Strait. The U.S.A. will be, from this point forward, known as "THE GUARDIAN OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT," but as such, and as a matter of FAIRNESS, will be reimbursed, at the rate of 20% on all cargo shipped, for any and all costs necessary to do the job of providing safety and security to this very volatile section of the World.
POTUS is absolutely right. Whoever provides secure and safe passage of commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz should be compensated for this service. Iran has always been the GUARDIAN of the Strait and will remain so FOREVER. 20% is of course too much. We will be fair
CENTCOM says two US service members were killed in Jordan while defending against Iranian strikes. The deaths push both sides towards an retaliatory language in which each threatens to multiply the cost of the other's next attack.
From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran.
Our defense doctrine is clear: eye for an eye. Any aggression against Iran, including our infrastructure, will compel a powerful and decisive response. Those who contribute to such aggression, whatever the kind of support, will also be considered as legitimate targets.
Iran-backed Houthi forces attack two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, extending the threat to shipping beyond Hormuz. Trump says he is considering a much larger attack on Iran. The confrontation now threatens two of the world's most important energy routes at the same time.
Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi: The US has violated the Islamabad memorandum by attacking civilian infrastructure and reimposing a naval blockade, threatening security and commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz [...] Iran warns that any country assisting or participating in attacks against it will bear international responsibility [...] the source of any attack against Iran will be considered a legitimate target for defensive action by its armed forces.
US military officials urge Trump to halt the bombing campaign as diplomats try to prevent another slide into all-out war. Iran frames the pause as proof that resistance has cost Washington. The de-escalation again takes the form of a unilateral operational pause rather than an agreed ceasefire, and oil prices fall.
Iran is not holding negotiations with the US [...] Talks are with Oman and are focused on arrangements for passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
After four days of strikes, the US and Iran agree to send delegations to Qatar, even as Tehran publicly denies holding direct talks with Washington. The apparent contradiction reflects the shape of the diplomacy: messages moved through Qatar, Pakistan and Oman while both sides avoid acknowledging concessions to the other.
The Doha talks fail to settle the central disputes. Trump again threatens heavy strikes, saying Iran would eventually decide it could no longer continue.
The US, Iran, Oman, Qatar and Pakistan pursue a wider settlement aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz. But the US blockade remains in place, commercial traffic is still constrained and the two sides continue to dispute who will control the waterway.
February daily average: 110
The U.S.A. is locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II. Despite this, we have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to. This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL. The Country of Israel joins me in this commitment. Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE.
Future management of the Strait of Hormuz will be led by Iran, in consultation with Oman and other regional countries [...] The northern route remained safe and open to shipping for the first 22–23 days of the agreement [...] but the US attacked Iran before the 30-day deadline for restoring maritime traffic to pre-war conditions.
Iran and Oman agree a proposed arrangement under which ships would enter the Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and leave through Omani waters. It is the most detailed reopening plan yet, but fees, security guarantees and the US blockade remain unresolved. Regional negotiations are advancing on a parallel track to the US-Iran talks.
"Massive attack coming… wait, never mind, they want to negotiate." That’s theater diplomacy on loop. Using bullying + broken promises + fake news as leverage is a failed strategy. Acknowledge the facts and fulfill your commitments. We don’t need more theater.
The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT! Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, "A WALL OF STEEL," and there is nothing Iran can do about it. They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, their remaining soldiers are unpaid, the IRGC is decimated and fleeing, and their "Leadership" is uncertain, at best! They have No Money - Their country is "shot." All they have is FAKE NEWS and 300% INFLATION, and getting worse! Iran is all talk and no action, the Bully of the Middle East No Longer. Praise be to Allah!
Donald Trump calls the strait of Hormuz “an American territory” while addressing a crowd in South Carolina. “We don’t even know if we won, because I view the strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now.”
We’ve received numerous messages from neighboring countries about shaping new security arrangements and economic cooperation in the region. The United States put the security of every single one of its allies at such risk through bullying and pure disregard for their interests for the sake of Israel that they briefly saw their entire existence on the line. A homegrown, independent order is what will actually deliver peace and security.
The Guardian looked at about 4,000 Truth Social posts, 7,700 IRGC Telegram messages and a selection of X posts from 28 February 2026. Some social media posts have been edited for conciseness. All times included in the piece are GMT.
Oil price data is sourced from LSEG. Data on the amount of shipping traffic through the strait of Hormuz is sourced from Lloyd’s List Intelligence, and only includes traceable transits of cargo-carrying vessels over 10,000 deadweight tonnage. Dark transits included in figures after 28 Feb.
Airstrikes data is sourced from Acled, and includes data on explosions or remote violence events, including air/drone strikes and shelling, artillery and missile attacks, by the Iranian, US and Israel military forces. It excludes interceptions.
